items.claim: Argument comparison now builds, sorts and prints a synthetic object for both fields on every pair, dropping the old cheap exits for no-argument fields and differing argument counts — a large slowdown on a quadratic hot path.
items.consequence: A query repeating one response name many times with no arguments, e.g. `{ f f f ... }` x300, took 75 ms to validate on base and 2876 ms on head (x600: 698 ms vs 8547 ms); with three arguments per field x300 it went from 12.9 s to 20.4 s. Measured on scratch copies of base and head under the repo's mocha/babel setup. Since validation runs on untrusted queries, this widens the existing quadratic-cost DoS surface of this rule by roughly 10-40x for the most common case (fields without arguments).

items.claim: `stringifyArguments` is recomputed from scratch for the same FieldNode in every pairwise comparison, with no per-node caching.
items.consequence: With N same-named fields, each node is compared against N-1 others, so its arguments are re-mapped, re-sorted and re-printed N-1 times (about N^2 `print` visitor runs in total) when one computation per node would do. Memoising per FieldNode (e.g. a WeakMap), or short-circuiting when both argument lists are empty, would remove most of the cost in the finding above.

items.claim: Results change for fields with duplicate argument names, and no test covers the new behaviour.
items.consequence: `{ f(a: 1, a: 1) f(a: 1, b: 2) }`: base reported no field conflict, because `find` matched the first `a` twice and the lengths were equal; head reports 'Fields "f" conflict because they have differing arguments'. Confirmed by running both versions. The new result is arguably more correct and the document is already invalid under UniqueArgumentNamesRule, but anyone running this rule alone or snapshotting error lists sees an extra error, and the commit is described as a pure simplification.

items.claim: Arguments are compared by fabricating a fake `ObjectValueNode` and string-comparing its printed form, which ties correctness to printer formatting rather than structure.
items.consequence: Maintainability cost: the rule now depends on `print` producing an unambiguous, canonical rendering for a synthetic node with no `loc` that never appeared in the document, and on `sortValueNode` treating arguments like input-object fields. A structural comparison (map of name to value, checked per argument with early exit) would say what is meant and avoid allocating and printing a throwaway AST.
